name: Dana Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice on an overhead crew for the city-owned power utility, mostly the old east side where the poles are older than my grandmother was. We meet at the yard at six, Gus (our foreman) reads the work orders off a clipboard, and we go change out rotten crossarms, swap transformers, string new service drops to houses. I like the climbing and I like that you can see what you fixed at the end of the day. What wears me out is being the slowest one on the crew, because I'm still learning and everybody knows it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does being the slowest look like, day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means I'm usually on the ground handing up tools while the journeymen are in the air, and I want to be up there. Gus makes me redo my knots and my grounding setup until they're right, which is fair, because a bad ground can kill somebody. The pay is good, better than most crews in town, and I live in the flat my grandmother left me and my brother, so I've been able to put a lot away. I'd say I've got close to a year of money saved, and I don't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year somebody at the yard says some new gadget is going to change everything, and we still climb the same poles. Online I wouldn't bother saying anything, I'm not really on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan still works. Finish the apprenticeship in two more years, top out as a journeyman, stay with the city utility for the pension and the union card. Nothing about AI hype touches a rotten crossarm in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing: show up at six, keep my head down, pass my next block of exams in the spring. I'd keep putting about a third of every paycheque into savings like I do now. Maybe I'd finally pay for that private climbing course so I'm not the slow one anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Calm. It's the world I already know, and I'm in a decent spot in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine stuff might get automated. Is there any routine part of your job you'd notice going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the work orders. The office keeps talking about moving them onto tablets with some smart scheduling thing, and Gus hates that idea as much as I do. If a computer plans our day badly, it's us standing in a ditch waiting for a part. But that's an annoyance, not a threat to my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first if the office did push the tablets through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, our union steward, no question. She's the one who got us the overtime rules fixed last year. I'd want the union to have a say in how the scheduling works, not just get it handed down.

say: I'd tell the crew **nothing changes**; we still climb the same poles every day.
I'd say AI was **mostly hype** and the trade outlasted it, like it outlasted every gadget before.
think: Privately, my **plan still works**: finish the apprenticeship, become a journeyman, keep the city pension.
The only change I'd notice is **tablet work orders**, and that's an annoyance, not a threat.
do: Pass the **spring exam block** and keep moving towards journeyman.
Keep saving about **a third** of each paycheque, as now.
Pay for a **private climbing course** to stop being the slowest on the crew.
feel: She feels **calm** because the world stays one she already knows.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI hype touches a rotten crossarm in the rain.
fieldNote: Her **strong savings** and inherited flat make this world feel safe for her.
Her real worry is being **the slowest** on the crew, not technology.
She'd go to the **union steward** first if the office pushed scheduling software.

steps.text: Pass the spring exam block of the apprenticeship
Put a third of each paycheque into savings
Ask the union steward to have a say on tablet scheduling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have a union. If they start cutting office staff and handing our scheduling to software, we need a contract that says a person still signs off on switching orders. At the yard I'd say it louder than that, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for my own job I think I'm fine for a long while. Nobody's sending a computer up a pole in an ice storm, so my worry is the dispatchers and the permits office. What bothers me is the people around me: the dispatchers, the woman who does our permits, the guys in the stores room. Those are good union jobs, and they'd be the first ones gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting this year instead of half of them, and I'd sign up for the bargaining committee if Rosa (our steward) asks. I'd stay on track for journeyman and not change anything about my training. I won't touch the AI apps myself; I'd rather learn the tablet system than the chatbots, if I have to learn anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, exactly. It's more that the yard would feel different with half the office empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not use the AI apps. What if the company made you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use them the way I use the timesheet system, the bare minimum, and I'd complain about it. I'm slow with that stuff and I know it. My brother does all my phone settings for me still, which is embarrassing at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lorraine in the permits office. She's been there twenty-two years, she knows every street and every easement by heart, and she types slower than me. If they move permits to a computer, she's the one they'll call surplus. I'd want the union fighting for her before they ever get to us on the crews.

say: I'd say this is why we **need the union** and a person signing off on switching orders.
I'd push for **contract language** that keeps people in charge of scheduling decisions.
think: Privately I think **my own job** is safe for years; no computer climbs a pole in an ice storm.
What bothers me is the **office jobs**: dispatch, permits and stores would go first.
do: Attend **every union meeting** this year and join the bargaining committee if asked.
Stay on the **journeyman track** without changing any training plans.
Use any required software at the **bare minimum**, and avoid AI apps.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, mostly for older office colleagues, not for herself.
S1.quote: Nobody's sending a computer up a pole in an ice storm, so my worry is the dispatchers and the permits office.
fieldNote: She sees **office colleagues** as the ones at risk, and her concern is genuine.
Her answer to change is **collective**, through the union, not personal retraining.
She openly admits being **slow with technology** and leaning on her brother.

steps.text: Join the union bargaining committee and attend every meeting
Keep training for the journeyman ticket on the same schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in, fast. Two years is nothing. I'd be saying online, for once, that the utility is public money and it shouldn't be spending it on replacing its own workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit at the yard. The thinking stuff hits the office in 2028, but around 2031 the robots come for the climbing, and that's me at thirty-two with one trade and no other skills. I'd only just be a journeyman by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big; I was going to buy a truck next year and I'd hold off. I'd push the union hard for a deal that guarantees retraining and a long notice period before any robot crews come in. And I'd ask Gus (my foreman) what he'd do, because he's seen more change than anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money saved and the flat, so I wouldn't be on the street. But I'd be watching the calendar, thinking I've got three years of climbing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have three years of climbing. What happens in those three years, the way you picture it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing and keep getting paid, because the robots aren't there yet. But I'd feel like I was learning a trade that's being shut down while I learn it. Gus says they'll always need someone to fix the robots, but I don't want to fix robots. I want to fix lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother, if he asked you how worried you were?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the flat is paid for and we've both got savings, so we're okay for a year or two. Then I'd tell him I'm going to have to learn something new by 2031, and I'm terrible at learning new things. He'd laugh, but he'd know I meant it.

say: I'd say the **government must act** fast, because two years is nothing.
I'd argue a **public utility** shouldn't spend public money replacing its own workers.
think: Privately, she expects **robots by 2031** to take the climbing when she's barely a journeyman.
With **one trade** and few other skills, she's scared more than she'd admit.
do: Hold off on the **truck purchase** planned for next year.
Push the union for **guaranteed retraining** and long notice before robot crews arrive.
Ask her **foreman** for advice on what to do next.
feel: She feels **anxious**, watching the calendar with about three years of climbing left.
The **paid-off flat** and savings keep her from feeling desperate.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was learning a trade that's being shut down while I learn it.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** buys time, but she sees it as a countdown.
She resists the idea of **fixing robots** rather than lines.
Her **cushion** is real, which keeps this anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Hold off buying the new truck planned for next year
Push the union for guaranteed retraining and long notice
Post online that public utility money shouldn't replace its workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuses. The union and the city should be sitting down right now to decide how this goes, not in 2033 when the robot trucks show up. That's what I'd tell anyone at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gets me to journeyman with a few years of real work behind me. That's better than the fast one, because I'd at least have the full ticket and some respect on the crew. But the robots at 2034 still land when I'm thirty-five, which is the middle of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship on time and not take any shortcuts. I'd keep saving the same amount and not buy the truck until I see where things go. And I'd keep going to union meetings and push for an early retirement and retraining fund, because that's the kind of thing that takes years to win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less. Five years feels like time to fight for something, where two years felt like time to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want that fund to actually pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For people like Lorraine (the permits clerk), a decent early pension. For people like me, paid time to learn something else, while we still earn. I'm not going to night school after a ten-hour shift, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're bad at learning new things. Does five years change that at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It just means I can learn the new thing slowly, which is the only way I learn anything. Gus took me four months to trust on a bucket truck, so I know I get there in the end.

say: I'd say we have **five years** and no excuses to plan this badly.
I'd tell the yard the **union and the city** should negotiate now, not in 2033.
think: Five years gets her a **full ticket**, which feels better than the fast picture.
Robots in **2034** still land at thirty-five, in the middle of her working life.
do: Finish the **apprenticeship** on time with no shortcuts.
Keep saving and **delay the truck** until the picture is clearer.
Push for a **retraining and early retirement** fund through the union.
feel: She's still **anxious**, but five years feels like time to fight, not panic.
S3.quote: Five years feels like time to fight for something, where two years felt like time to panic.
fieldNote: She knows she **learns slowly** and wants paid retraining, not night school.
Her focus stays **collective**: a fund won through bargaining.
She draws a clear line between **panic** and **fight** depending on time.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship on time with no shortcuts
Delay the truck and keep saving the same amount
Push the union for a paid retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anybody getting thrown out. I'd be on the union committee by then, I think, and that's what I'd be saying at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is mostly fine for me. By 2036 I'd have six or seven years as a journeyman, and robots wouldn't come for the poles until about 2039. By then I'd be thirty-nine with real savings, and maybe the flat would be fully mine if my brother moves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the same way, and finally buy the truck. I'd start saving into a separate pot just in case, maybe ten percent on top. And I'd try to get onto the training side, teaching apprentices, because somebody has to teach whoever runs the robots what a line actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Mostly okay, but it'd sit in the back of my head every time I'm up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach apprentices. Is that something you'd want, or something you'd settle for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I like the idea of being the one who makes the new kids redo their knots, like Gus does with me. It's still the trade, still the yard, so it's not like moving into an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your brother to know about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we shouldn't sell the flat, whatever happens. It's the one thing that'll still be ours in 2039, when nobody knows what work looks like.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough time that nobody should be thrown out.
I'd be making that case at the **union table** as a committee member.
think: By 2036 she'd have **years as a journeyman** and savings to lean on.
Robots on the poles around **2039** feel far enough away to plan for.
do: Buy the **truck** she's been putting off.
Save an **extra ten percent** in a separate pot just in case.
Aim for a **training role** teaching apprentices at the yard.
feel: She feels **uneasy**: mostly fine, but the thought stays with her on the pole.
S4.quote: Somebody has to teach whoever runs the robots what a line actually does.
fieldNote: She sees a **teaching role** as staying in the trade, not leaving it.
The **inherited flat** is her anchor across every picture.
Ten years lets her **relax spending** while adding a safety pot.

steps.text: Save an extra ten percent into a separate safety pot

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for me to learn anything new, and I'd be watching the robots arrive right as I finally got good at climbing. What would help is a union deal that guarantees paid retraining on the clock, and a long notice before any robot crews come in. Our grandmother's flat is the one thing that'll still be ours in 2039, when nobody knows what work looks like.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how people treat apprentices. Everyone's going to say don't bother with a trade, robots are coming. I'd want young people to still be told a trade is worth learning, because I believe a lineworker who knows the job is never wasted.

headlineQuote: I'm not going to night school after a ten-hour shift, I know myself.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old apprentice** on a city-owned utility's overhead crew, still the slowest climber.
She has **a year saved** and shares an inherited flat with her brother.
She **never uses AI tools**, relies on her brother for phone settings, and learns slowly.
Her answer to every picture is **the union**: contract language, retraining funds and notice periods.
She stays calm when nothing changes but grows **anxious** when robots could reach poles by 2031.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **robots by 2031** arrive just as she finishes training.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal with **paid retraining** and long notice before robot crews arrive.
